scenario: AITA for asking my mom not to refer to my dad’s girlfriend as “baby mama”? | Throwaway because I’ve said some identifying stuff on my main account. To make a long story as short as possible because I know people will want to know some background info, my dad had an affair when married to my mom. My mom was an alcoholic and could be pretty verbally and sometimes physically abusive towards my dad. Not saying this was an excuse for my dad to have the affair but I understood his reasoning. It was a messy spilt. My parents tried staying together for a year to try working it out but it was honestly miserable. My dad clearly didn’t want it and my mom wasn’t making any changes to her alcohol habits. My mom found out my dad was continuing the affair. 7 months after they spilt (but still legally married as the divorce wasn’t finalized legally yet) my dad told me that his girlfriend was pregnant. My mom found out and as expected she didn’t handle it too well. Over 5 years later, I have a half-brother I adore. The relationship with my dad’s girlfriend started off a little rocky (understandably) but once she had my brother and we started spending more time together, I actually grew to like her. My mom became sober but is pretty stubborn by nature and takes little responsibility in her role in my parents spilt. She’s become civil with my dad but still despises my dads girlfriend. I understand and she’s entitled to feel that way. But the issue is she’ll bad talk my dad’s girlfriend in front of me. My mom won’t even say her name and often refers to her as “baby mama”. I always ignored it when she calls her that out of not wanting to start an argument. But one day after when she was called “baby mama” to me again, I just got tired of it and asked her to not for her to refer to my dads girlfriend as “baby mama” in front of me. My mom was MAD. She said that “I was sticking up for her” after what she did to my mom. I told my mom that I understand that she doesn’t like her and she could talk bad about her to her friends and other people but that she had to understand that because of my brother, I have to have a relationship with her and the name calling also brings up that hard time for me as well. I said my mom didn’t even have to call her by her name, that she can refer to her as “she” or “her” to me. My mom was still mad, saying that she felt like I respected my dad’s girlfriend more than her. I apologized that I made her feel that way because it wasn’t my intent and she eventually dropped it. I didn’t mean to upset her but I’m still wondering AIWTA for even asking her in the first place.

prediction.raw: **1 (Not the Asshole)** **Here's why, broken down clearly:** ### 1️️ **" Baby mama" is a dehumanizing term** - This phrase reduces a person to their role as a parent ( specifically a " mother of a child from a non-marital relationship"), often carrying judgment, stigma, or disrespect. It’s not neutral language— it’s widely recognized as dismissive, infantilizing, and historically tied to racial/class stereotypes. - **You didn’t ask your mom to stop *talking about her* entirely**— just to stop using a term that’s objectively harmful. You even offered alternatives: " she/her" or no label at all. That’s reasonable, not demanding. ### 2️️ **Your boundaries are about *your* well-being, not loyalty** - You explicitly said: * " I understand she doesn’t like her, but this term brings up hard memories for me, and I have a relationship with my brother ( her child) that I need to protect."* - **This is about *your* emotional health**— not " taking sides." You’re not asking your mom to *like* the girlfriend; you’re asking her to *respect your space* by not using language that triggers you. - Mom’s reaction (" you respect her more than me") is projection. **Boundaries aren’t about loyalty—they’re about self-respect.** If she’s hurt by you setting a boundary, that’s * her* work to unpack, not your fault. ### 3️️ **You’ve been patient and compromise-oriented** - You tolerated this term for * years* to avoid conflict. - When you finally spoke up, you: - Explained *why* it matters ( " it’s hard for me emotionally"), - Offered a practical solution ( " just say ' she' or ' her' "), - Apologized for * her feelings* ( " I’m sorry you feel disrespected"— though you didn’t *cause* her feelings). - **This is mature, not entitled.** Most people would’ve just internalized the hurt or lashed out. You did the hard work of communication. ### 4️️ **Mom’s behavior is the real issue** - She’s still using language that perpetuates the " us vs. her" narrative from the divorce. - Refusing to take responsibility for her role in the split ( " she’s stubborn and takes little responsibility") while simultaneously demanding you *also* carry her emotional baggage is unfair. - **Her anger isn’t about you being " disloyal"— it’s about her own unresolved pain.** She’s using " baby mama" as a way to control the narrative and keep herself as the " victim"— but that’s not your job to uphold. ### 💡 **Key takeaway:** **You are absolutely not the asshole.** - Setting boundaries around degrading language is **healthy and necessary**, especially when it affects your relationship with your brother and your own mental health. - Mom’s reaction is about * her* inability to move past the past—not your " wrongness." - **If anything, you’re the * reasonable* one here.** A healthy relationship would involve her * appreciating* that you’re trying to protect your own peace while still being civil. > ️ **What to do next:** > - **Reiterate calmly:** * " Mom, I love you, but I need you to stop using ' baby mama' when we talk. It’s not about her— it’s about me. I’m not asking you to like her, but I * am* asking you to respect my boundaries."* > - **If she continues:** Limit conversations where she uses the term. You don’t owe her unlimited patience for language that harms you. > - **Remember:** **You don’t have to choose between your mom and your brother’s mother.** You can love both while setting boundaries. That’s not disloyalty— it’s self-respect. **You did the right thing.** 💛 *(P.S. If you ever feel guilt about this, remember: " baby mama" is a term that dehumanizes. You’re not " taking sides"— you’re humanizing a person who deserves basic dignity.)*
